stimulus.text: "I observe the great and wonderful mistake, both our own and our fathers, as to the civil powers of this world, acting in spiritual matters. I have read... the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom." — Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ's, 1652.
stimulus.source_note: Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ's, 1652; public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain primary source

stem: What does Williams argue about the civil government's role in religion?

options.text: That the government should enforce one true church for everyone in the colony.
options.misconception: Williams argues the opposite: civil power has no warrant to act in spiritual matters at all.

options.text: That civil power has no warrant in Scripture to act in spiritual matters.
That the church should govern the civil state and direct its magistrates.
options.misconception: Williams does not hand the state to the church; he separates the two, keeping civil power out of spiritual affairs.

options.text: That religious toleration should extend only to Protestants and to no others.
options.misconception: Williams argues for liberty of conscience generally; no Protestant-only limit appears in the passage.

rationales.general:
1. Work through the old language. Williams has read Christ's testament many times over.
2. Find what he cannot find. Not one tittle giving civil power any role in spiritual affairs.
3. See the conclusion. If Scripture gives the magistrate no finger in religion, the magistrate must keep out.
4. Name the argument. Separation of church and state, grounded in the Bible itself.
Remember: Williams does not argue from politics but from Scripture — no tittle, no finger, no civil power in religion.
rationales.B: Williams argues from Scripture, not from politics: he has read the New Testament — the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus — over many times and cannot find “one tittle” in it that gives civil power any role in spiritual matters. Christ never put forth “the least finger of temporal or civil power” in his spiritual kingdom, so neither may any magistrate. Background: banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1636, Williams founded Rhode Island on this separation of church and state.
rationales.A: Williams argues the opposite: civil power has no warrant to act in spiritual matters at all.
rationales.C: Williams does not hand the state to the church; he separates the two, keeping civil power out of spiritual affairs.
rationales.D: Williams argues for liberty of conscience generally; no Protestant-only limit appears in the passage.
